paras: The attempted lynching of William Spencer occurred on June 15, 1903, in the Criminal Courts Building in New York City, when a crowd of men tried to take Spencer, a Black man, from a detective minutes after he shot and killed Charles F. McFarlane of the Anti-Policy Society. Police held the crowd back, and Spencer was indicted for first-degree murder within about two hours. He was convicted and sentenced to death the next month, and the Court of Appeals confirmed the conviction in November 1904. Wire stories outside New York presented the episode as a near-lynching in a northern courthouse, under headlines such as "Tried to Lynch the Murderer."

Spencer, about thirty-five, was due in court that morning for trial on a charge of having policy slips, a violation of the anti-policy law. The Sun reported that McFarlane had arrested him on May 11 for running a policy game in the West Side's Black tenements, and that McFarlane and agent Philip E. Bray were to testify against him. According to the New-York Tribune, Spencer had told McFarlane the previous Friday that he would never take the stand against him, and McFarlane had told a friend he feared being shot.

Shortly before 11 a.m., McFarlane and Bray stepped off an elevator on the crowded second floor, where Spencer was waiting. After a brief exchange, Spencer drew a revolver and fired four shots; three struck McFarlane, who died at once, and the fourth wounded Bray in the arm. Officers in the building seized Spencer and knocked or wrenched the pistol from him, though the Tribune and the Sun named different men as his captors.

According to the wire account, a crowd of men from the emptied courtrooms, crying "Lynch him!" and "Throw him over the balcony!", tried to take the prisoner from the detective until a strong force of police dispersed them. The Worcester Spy's version added that the men fought fiercely to reach Spencer, that a dozen policemen surrounded him, and that the crowd broke up only when another squad arrived.

While he was being arraigned that afternoon, the Evening Star reported, a great crowd around the building raised fresh cries of "Lynch the nigger!" and blocked the Centre Street cars, and prisoners in the Toombs joined the uproar. Spencer told police that McFarlane had been hounding him, and the Sun reported that he claimed at headquarters to have acted in self-defence.

The grand jury indicted Spencer for first-degree murder within about an hour, and Recorder Goff assigned ex-Judge Wauhope Lynn as his counsel. No arrests of anyone in the crowd appear in the coverage. At trial his lawyers argued insanity, with four doctors testifying for the defence and two for the prosecution, and the jury was out about an hour. Spencer was convicted of first-degree murder on the night of July 9 and sentenced to death in the week beginning August 17. On November 22, 1904, the Court of Appeals confirmed the conviction.

Papers outside New York carried the story under lynching headlines: the Evening Star's "Threatened With Lynching," the Worcester Spy's "Tried to Lynch the Murderer," and the Omaha Daily Bee's "Nearly Lynched by New Yorkers." These versions called Spencer "the negro," printed the crowd's slur, and described him as looking like "the typical Tenderloin negro."

The New York papers framed it differently. The Evening World's same-day headline was "Policy Murder Finds a Swift Retribution," the Tribune's was "Policy Player Kills" over "Indicted Hour Later," and the Sun's was "Negro Kills Goddard Agent." They dwelt on Spencer's record and threats and the speed of the indictment, treated the crowd as an uproar rather than a lynch mob; the Tribune quoted McFarlane calling Spencer "that coon."

In the Black press, the Cleveland Gazette ran a single wire paragraph on the shooting in its news digest on June 20, with no mention of the crowd and no comment. No other Black-press coverage was found.

Only the wire accounts report an attempt to seize Spencer or cries to lynch him. The Tribune and the Sun, the most detailed local accounts, describe a crowd of about five hundred that police struggled to move along, but neither mentions lynching nor denies an attempt.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of William Spencer
bases: An attempted lynching: wire reports say a crowd of men crying 'Lynch him!' tried to take Spencer, held for a killing minutes earlier, from a detective and was held back by police (A2, A3); he was not harmed.

A crowd of men crying 'Lynch him!' tried to seize Spencer for the killing of McFarlane (A2, A3), a group acting on a pretext of punishment, but police held them back and no one in the coverage reports Spencer killed or injured; he was tried, convicted and sentenced by a court (A14, A16).

The shooting, arrest and swift indictment are reported alike by the wire and both New York local papers (A2, A4, A5); the attempt to seize Spencer appears in two differently worded wire versions (A2, A3), while the two detailed local accounts describe a large, shoving crowd but no cries to lynch (A4, A5).

accounts.label: Wire report (Evening Star version)
accounts.gist: A crowd of men crying 'Lynch him!' and 'Throw him over the balcony!' tried to take Spencer from the detective and a strong police force was needed to save him; during arraignment a great crowd outside cried 'Lynch the nigger!'

accounts.label: Wire report (Worcester Spy version)
accounts.gist: Men fought fiercely to reach Spencer; a dozen policemen surrounded him and the crowd was dispersed only when another squad arrived; 'police alone saved' him.

accounts.label: New York local papers
accounts.gist: About five hundred people packed the corridor and police had trouble moving them along (Tribune); a 'curious and shoving, loud-talking crowd' followed as officers took Spencer to the basement cells (Sun); neither reports cries to lynch.

accounts.label: Spencer's statements to police
accounts.gist: McFarlane had been 'hounding' him, telling lies and threatening him; he said he would as soon go to the electric chair, and at headquarters he claimed McFarlane made a motion as if to shoot and that he acted in self-defence.

framing.detail: Out-of-town papers ran the wire under lynching headlines ('Threatened With Lynching', 'Tried to Lynch the Murderer', 'Nearly Lynched by New Yorkers'), calling Spencer 'the negro' and printing the crowd's slur.

The New York papers headlined the murder and the swift indictment ('Policy Player Kills. Indicted Hour Later.', 'Negro Kills Goddard Agent', 'Policy Murder Finds a Swift Retribution') and treated the crowd as an uproar, not a lynch mob; they used 'negro' and quoted McFarlane calling Spencer 'that coon'.
The Cleveland Gazette carried only the shooting paragraph in a news digest, without the lynching attempt or comment.

record_check.dossier: Attempted: a crowd tried to seize Spencer and was held back by police; not a lynching by the standard definition.
Spencer is described as 'a negro' in every account.

record_check.record: accused of violating the anti-policy law
record_check.dossier: The crowd's grievance was the shooting and killing of Charles F. McFarlane in the courthouse; the policy charge was the case he was about to be tried on.
Attempted seizure and threats only; the shooting was Spencer's, of McFarlane and Bray, not the crowd's.
Not taken: the crowd tried to take him from a detective but police prevented it.

record_check.record: resisting the attack of a gang of hoodlums
record_check.dossier: None stated by the crowd; the record's phrase comes from an unrelated editorial (A10) about police shooting Black men in New York, not this episode.
One white man killed and one wounded by Spencer before the crowd formed; none by the crowd.

At least seven white papers opened (New York, Washington, Worcester, Omaha, Wheeling) plus follow-ups to Nov. 1904, and one Black paper (Cleveland Gazette); the record's second white item (A10) is not about this episode.

info: Second-floor (general sessions) corridor of the Criminal Courts Building, Centre Street, New York City; later crowds outside the building during arraignment
William Spencer (also known as William Rogers), described as 'a negro', about 35, of 224 West Twenty-ninth Street; target of the crowd, not reported injured

Shooting and killing Charles F. McFarlane (Macfarlane), superintendent of the Anti-Policy Society, and wounding Philip E. Bray; Spencer was in court to be tried on a charge of violating the anti-policy law (having policy slips)
Unnamed men from the crowd that poured out of the courtrooms into the corridors; later a crowd outside the building
Sentenced by Recorder Goff to death in the week beginning Aug. 17, 1903; conviction confirmed by the Court of Appeals Nov. 22, 1904
